Esperanto actually has very little benefit, except for being an interesting historical relic. While it was invented to be a universal second language, it has a couple of significant shortcomings. It's modeled heavily on Western European languages, largely ignoring the structure of the other major world languages. So it's easier to learn for French, Spanish, Italian, and English speakers, but not so much for Hebrew, Japanese, or Swahili speakers.

Its treatment of gender endings is also off-putting. Basically to form a feminine, you add the suffix 'ino'. So father is 'patro' and mother is 'patrino.' Notice that father is a lot like the romance language form (padre, pater, etc.), but the romance language form of 'mother' (mater, madre, etc.) just disappears. And that 'ino' suffix is very similar to the diminutive suffix in a few languages. So the word for mother is effectively 'little father.' Kind of offensive to formalize a gender bias in language.

I've dabbled, but there's little reason to do so beyond it being kind of a nifty thought exercise. I'm not sure there's a whole lot of benefit, really, and I'm definitely a language geek. I've seen it suggested that it's a good second language in that it starts training you to learn others, but I don't really think that's true (Spanish is my second language, and I didn't have any trouble learning it despite no exposure to Esperanto until much later). In some ways its ease of use might spoil you - after all, the whole point was to make an incredibly simple language.

A basic grammar can fit on an index card. Nouns always end in o, adjectives in a, and adverbs in e. For a plural, add a j on the end of the o or a (and a plural noun needs a plural adjective). Direct objects of the sentence also get an n. Verbs only change for tense, not for person (present -as, past -is, future -os, conditional -us, infinitive -i). Roots can generally be switched between them without issue. So you can have Mi bonas (I am well), to referring to something as bona (or multiple things as bonaj), to doing something well with bone.

The criticisms about it being too Western-centric are definitely legit, although it does certainly make it easier to learn if you're a native speaker of a Romance language or English. Every once in a blue moon it has a word that seems kind of out there to me as an English speaker. For example, flava is the Esperanto word for "yellow," which is the same in Latin, but most Romance languages use something else. But most of the time it's pretty obvious where the word came from (such as the bon stem in my examples above). "To drink" is trinki, "learn" is lerni, "blue" is *blua," etc.

I have fun with it. I participate a bit in the Esperanto section of that other website, there’s a good community over there.

There’s an oft referenced study, where they took students and put them in two groups. The first group learned French for 4 years. The second learned Esperanto for 1 year and then French for 3. At the end, the second group spoke better French. It seems it’s good for language learning to have a base to build upon that has no distractions of language exceptions and illogical rules.

A flashcard program like Anki is great for building up your vocabulary, and getting your favorite book in Esperanto is wonderful for a measure of immersion. My brother gifted me a copy of “La Hobito”, or “The Hobbit” in Esperanto, along with an Esperanto dictionary (though you can find good ones online).
